key_insight: Grouping IoT temperature sensors into Communities of Interest (CoIs) using a fused similarity matrix enables community-level model sharing, improving anomaly detection generalisation across heterogeneous deployments.
problem_solved: Detecting anomalies in large, heterogeneous IoT sensor networks is hard because devices operate in diverse environments and labelled anomalies are scarce; this work addresses scalable, generalisable anomaly detection by organising sensors into similar communities and sharing models between them.
method: Build a fused similarity matrix combining temporal patterns, spatial proximity, and device/operational metadata to cluster sensors into Communities of Interest (CoIs).
Train community-level anomaly detectors (unsupervised or semi-supervised) and enable model sharing/transfer across CoIs to improve detection in under-labelled or new deployments.
Evaluate generalisation by transferring models between communities and measuring anomaly detection performance gains compared to isolated per-device models.
impact: Practitioners can reduce labelling effort and improve robustness of anomaly detection in distributed IoT deployments by leveraging community structures and model sharing, making scalable monitoring more practical for real-world sensor networks.
visual_elements: Schematic of sensors on a map colour-coded into Communities of Interest (CoIs).
Diagram showing construction of fused similarity matrix (temporal, spatial, metadata) and community clustering.
Flowchart of model training and sharing: community-level training → model transfer/adaptation → anomaly detection output.
Time-series plot with detected anomalies annotated, comparing standalone vs. community-shared model performance.
paper_title: Community-Based Model Sharing and Generalisation: Anomaly Detection in IoT Temperature Sensor Networks
paper_authors: Sahibzada Saadoon Hammad, Joaquín Huerta Guijarro, Francisco Ramos, Michael Gould Carlson, Sergio Trilles Oliver
